title: The Awakenings and the Birth of Evangelicalism
subtitle: Pietism, Edwards, Whitefield, and the Wesleys. How revival remade the faith of the English-speaking world, with the ledger of the revivalists and slavery kept open and honest.

sections.title: After the Wars, the Chill
sections.body:
When the religious wars burned out, much of Protestant Europe settled into a faith that was correct and cold. The state churches had confessions nobody disputed and pews nobody warmed with much feeling. Theologians defended orthodoxy with precision while the educated classes drifted toward a politer religion, a distant God who had built the clock and wound it and did not interfere, and who would certainly never demand anything so indecent as a new birth. The age called this reasonableness. Later believers would call it sleep.

What broke the sleep was not an argument. Between the 1730s and the 1740s, on both sides of the Atlantic, ordinary congregations began to experience something their grandparents would have recognized from the Reformation and their pastors could not fully control. Conviction of sin. Public weeping. Conversions in numbers no one could count, among farmhands and colliers and merchants and the enslaved. The people it touched called it an outpouring of the Spirit, a surprising work of God. Its critics called it enthusiasm, and they did not mean it kindly.

Out of those years came a new thing with an old heart, the movement we now call evangelicalism, a Christianity organized less around state churches and settled parishes than around conversion, the Bible, the cross, and the drive to spread the message, the four marks the historian David Bebbington taught us to look for. This essay tells how it was born, through Pietist Germany, a Massachusetts parsonage, and two Oxford friends who took to preaching in open fields. And it tells, without flinching, the sin the movement carried from its birth.

sections.title: Halle, Herrnhut, and the Religion of the Heart
sections.body:
The awakening had a German mother. In 1675 a Frankfurt pastor named Philipp Jakob Spener published Pia Desideria, a small book arguing that the Reformation had reformed doctrine but not lives, and proposing something scandalous in its simplicity. Small groups of laypeople would meet to read Scripture, pray, and hold one another to holiness. The movement his book named, Pietism, took institutional shape under August Hermann Francke at Halle, where an orphanage, a university, and a publishing operation grew into a working model of faith with its sleeves rolled up.

The strangest and most consequential Pietist community gathered on the estate of Count Nicolaus von Zinzendorf, where refugees from Moravia settled the village of Herrnhut. After a renewal there in 1727, the community began a prayer watch that members kept going around the clock for decades, and then it did something no Protestant body had seriously attempted. It sent missionaries. From 1732, Moravian craftsmen carried the gospel to enslaved Africans in the Caribbean and to Greenland, sixty years before the English societies existed.

The Moravians matter to this story for one more reason. In 1735 a rigid young Anglican priest named John Wesley sailed for Georgia and met a company of them aboard ship. When a storm split the mainsail and the English passengers screamed, the Moravians calmly sang psalms, their women and children included, and Wesley, who discovered in that hour that he was afraid to die, understood that they had something he did not. He went home a failed missionary with a question lodged in him. The answer came in 1738, in a room on Aldersgate Street.

sections.title: Edwards and the Surprising Work
sections.body:
Jonathan Edwards was the pastor of Northampton, Massachusetts, and very likely the finest mind America had yet produced, when in the winter of 1734 his town began to be surprised. Conversions multiplied until the revival was the only subject in the streets. His careful account of it, published in 1737 as a faithful narrative of a surprising work of God, circulated through Britain and kindled expectation wherever it went. When George Whitefield toured New England in 1740, the scattered fires became the Great Awakening, and for two years the colonies talked of little else.

Edwards became the awakening's theologian, and he refused to flatter it. Enthusiasm produced counterfeits, and he knew it. One traveling preacher, James Davenport, led bonfires of books and fine clothes in 1743 and later published a retraction of his own excesses. Edwards answered the chaos with Religious Affections in 1746, arguing that true religion lies neither in high emotion nor in cool correctness but in a changed heart that shows itself in a changed life. It remains the most searching test of revival ever written.

His own story ends with a lesson the movement needed. In 1750 the congregation he had served for more than two decades dismissed him in a bitter dispute over who should come to the Lord's table. He went quietly to the frontier at Stockbridge as a missionary to the Mohican and Mohawk peoples, wrote his greatest philosophical works in near exile, accepted the presidency of the college at Princeton, and died in 1758, weeks into the office, from a smallpox inoculation. Revival had not made his people kind. That fact deserves a long pause.

sections.title: Whitefield, the Wesleys, and the Fields
sections.body:
George Whitefield could be heard. Shut out of Bristol's pulpits in early 1739, he preached in the open air to the Kingswood coal miners and wrote of tears cutting white channels down their coal-blackened faces. For the next thirty years he crossed the Atlantic thirteen times and preached to crowds no building could hold. In Philadelphia the skeptical Benjamin Franklin, who loved the man and doubted the message, once walked away from a sermon measuring the reach of his voice, did the arithmetic, and concluded that thirty thousand people could hear him at once. He was arguably the most famous man in the English-speaking world, and he spent the fame on eternity, preaching until days before he died at Newburyport in 1770.

John Wesley did not have Whitefield's voice. He had order. After his heart was strangely warmed, as his journal puts it, at a meeting on Aldersgate Street in May of 1738, and after Whitefield talked him into the indignity of field preaching, Wesley organized the awakened into societies, the societies into classes that met weekly, and the whole into a connection served by lay preachers he deployed like a general. He rode the roads of Britain for fifty years, preaching almost daily into his eighties. His brother Charles gave the movement its songs, writing hymns by the thousand that put the theology into the people's mouths, where it stayed.

The two friends split over predestination, Whitefield the Calvinist, Wesley the Arminian, and their followers said bitter things. The men themselves patched the friendship, and at Whitefield's own request, John Wesley preached his memorial sermon. It was a better ending than most theological quarrels get.

sections.title: The Revival and the Enslaved
sections.body:
Now the ledger the movement's admirers long refused to open. The awakeners preached the new birth in a world built on slavery, and most of them made their peace with it. Whitefield did worse than make peace. When the colony of Georgia, which had banned slavery, debated its introduction, he campaigned for legalization to supply labor for his Bethesda orphanage, and after the ban fell in 1751 he bought human beings and worked them. He rebuked planters for cruelty and taught the enslaved the faith, and he died owning around fifty people, whom his will passed on like furniture. Edwards, the theologian of true holiness, bought and owned enslaved people and defended the practice in writing, though he condemned the ocean trade. The revival's clearest sight came with a blind spot the size of a person.

It must also be said that the gospel escaped its preachers. Enslaved men and women heard the message of the new birth and took it for themselves, on its own terms, and the awakening is where the African American church begins. George Liele, converted in Georgia and ordained in 1775, planted churches among the enslaved around Savannah and carried the gospel to Jamaica in the early 1780s, a decade before England's famous missionary society existed. Olaudah Equiano, once enslaved, published the story of his life and his faith in 1789, and it helped turn a nation against the trade.

And the movement's own logic worked on it. John Wesley attacked slavery outright in 1774, his societies listed slave trading among the sins a member must renounce, and the last letter he wrote, six days before his death in 1791, urged young William Wilberforce to press on against a trade he called a scandal to religion and to human nature.

sections.title: What Was Born, and What It Could Not See
sections.body:
Step back and look at what those sixty years produced. A Christianity of conversion rather than mere custom, carried by hymns, cheap print, and lay preachers, crossing denominational and national borders as if they were hedgerows. The missionary movement of the next century was its direct child. So was abolitionism. So was the black church. So, less happily, was a durable temptation to measure God's work by crowd size and feeling, which has dogged the movement ever since. Revival is power, and power always arrives without instructions.

No life holds the era's two truths together like John Newton's. Converted in a storm at sea in 1748, he went on captaining slave ships for six more years, Bible on his desk, human beings in his hold, and saw no contradiction. The seeing came slowly, as it usually does. Years later, as a pastor, he wrote the hymn about amazing grace and the wretch it saved, and in 1788 he published a confession of his part in the trade and testified against it while it still had teeth. He lived just long enough to see Parliament abolish the British slave trade in 1807.

That is the awakening in one man. Real grace, really received, coexisting for years with a monstrous blindness, and then, slowly, sight. It should make a modern believer neither cynical nor comfortable. The revivalists' God was not fooled by their revivals, and he is not fooled by ours. What was born in those years was alive, genuinely alive. But alive is not the same as whole, and the church is still learning the difference.

keyFigures.name: Jonathan Edwards
keyFigures.note: Northampton pastor and the awakening's theologian, author of Religious Affections.

keyFigures.name: George Whitefield
keyFigures.note: The awakening's voice, field preacher to tens of thousands, and a slaveholder.

keyFigures.name: John Wesley
keyFigures.note: Organizer of Methodism, awakened at Aldersgate in 1738, foe of slavery at the end.

keyFigures.name: Charles Wesley
keyFigures.note: Hymn writer of the movement, whose songs carried its theology into common memory.

keyFigures.name: Nicolaus von Zinzendorf
keyFigures.note: Moravian count whose Herrnhut community sent the first Protestant missionaries.

keyFigures.name: George Liele
keyFigures.note: Formerly enslaved preacher who planted churches in Georgia and carried the gospel to Jamaica.

keyFigures.name: John Newton
keyFigures.note: Slave-ship captain turned pastor, writer of the hymn on amazing grace, late witness against the trade.
